documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                          )
Midcontinent Independent System                           )                         Docket No. ER27-25-000
Operator, Inc.                                            )
                                                          )

                       MOTION TO INTERVENE AND COMMENTS OF
                               GERONIMO POWER, LLC

        Pursuant to Rules 212 and 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”

or “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure1 and the Commission’s October 2, 2026

Combined Notice of Filings #1,2 Geronimo Power, LLC (“Geronimo Power”) hereby submits this

motion to intervene and comments in the above-captioned proceeding concerning the

Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.’s (“MISO”) Large Load Addition Resource

Study Process (“LARS”) proposal.3

I.      COMMENTS

        Geronimo Power appreciates MISO’s efforts to develop interconnection processes that

facilitate the integration of large loads and respond to the directives included in the Commission’s

Show Cause Order.4 At a time when the MISO region is experiencing “significant growth in

electricity demand”5 and is “[t]he region with the fastest data center capacity growth” in the

country,6 it is imperative that MISO have processes that ensure large loads and generation capacity



        1
           18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.214.
        2
           Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., et al., Docket Nos. ER27-25-000, et al., Combined Notice of
Filings #1 (Oct. 2, 2026).
         3
           Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Docket No. ER27-25-000, Large Load Addition Resource Study
Process (Oct. 2, 2026) (“LARS Filing”).
         4
           Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,212, at P 2 (2026) (“Show Cause Order”).
         5
           LARS Filing, Transmittal Letter at 2.
         6
           FERC, 2025 State of the Markets Report at 7 (Mar. 2026), available at: https://www.ferc.gov/news-
events/news/report-3-state-markets-report-2025.
 serving these customers may interconnect to the grid in an efficient, timely, and non-discriminatory

manner.

        Geronimo Power supports the creation of efficient and non-discriminatory procedures that

provide for the coordinated study of new generation capacity and large load customers. Evaluating

paired generation capacity and large load can provide a more accurate picture of the net impact of

these customers on the transmission system and reduce the need for costly network upgrades that

can unnecessarily drive up costs and delay energization timelines. By reducing barriers to entry

to new generation and large load customers, interconnection procedures that provide for the

coordinated evaluation of generation and large loads can play a critical role in providing large

loads a pathway to power that maintains America’s economic competitiveness while

simultaneously mitigating impacts to the grid and avoiding cost shifts to existing customers.

        Nevertheless, any proposal that provides certain customers with a separate path to

interconnection service must comply with the Federal Power Act’s (“FPA”) prohibition on undue

discrimination and preference and open access requirements.7 Historically, the Commission has

been skeptical of any proposals that create a separate or expedited path for certain resources to

obtain interconnection service.8 But the Commission has approved expedited processes in limited

circumstances where such processes were narrowly tailored to meet a demonstrated reliability need

and “aligned with . . . open access principles in an objective and transparent manner.”9




        7
           Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 191 FERC ¶ 61,131, at PP 201-02 (2025). See also Cal. Indep.
Sys. Operator Corp., 180 FERC ¶ 61,143, at P 41 (2022); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,084, at P 248
(2025).
         8
           Xcel Energy Operating Co., 106 FERC ¶ 61,260, at PP 22-23 (2004); Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 147 FERC ¶
61,201, at P 124 (2014); Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 185 FERC ¶ 61,200, at PP 176-177 (2023).
         9
           Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 191 FERC ¶ 61,131, at PP 201-03 (2025). See also Cal. Indep.
Sys. Operator Corp., 180 FERC ¶ 61,143, at P 41 (2022); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,084, at P 248
(2025).

                                                       2
         MISO’s LARS proposal does not meet this standard. As currently conceived, LARS would

provide incumbent utilities with undue influence over the ability of interconnection customers to

access the process. Notably, an interconnection customer will not be able to participate in LARS

unless the interconnecting transmission owner “pre-approves” its proposed point of

interconnection and a MISO transmission customer—which typically will be a transmission owner

and load-serving entity (“LSE”)—submits an application into the LARS process.10 The result is a

framework that will provide incumbent utilities with new opportunities to discriminate against

competing suppliers and secure preferential access to interconnection service for their own

generation resources. Ultimately, this will provide incumbent utilities with a powerful tool that

they can use to pressure large load customers to rely on their generation resources, which will be

eligible to receive interconnection service more quickly and at lower cost than competing resources

that have been relegated to the standard interconnection queue.

        At the same time, certain aspects of MISO’s proposed framework appear to arbitrarily

exclude from LARS generation resources that are being developed to meet the demand of large

load customers in a manner that supports resource adequacy and protects ratepayers. For instance,

the requirement that an interconnection customer provide an offtake agreement demonstrating that

its facility will be used to provide energy to large load customers would appear to prevent a

generation resource that has entered into a virtual power purchase agreement (“PPA”) with a large

load customer from participating in LARS. Additionally, MISO’s description of the scope of

LARS could be interpreted as prohibiting co-located generation and load from accessing the LARS


        10
             Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 170 FERC ¶ 61,215, at P 13 (2020) (“[A]pproximately 90% of
the load in MISO is served by vertically integrated LSEs[.]”); Entergy Ark., LLC v. Webb, Case No. 24-1074, Brief of
Amicus Curiae the MISO Transmission Owners Supporting Petitioner at 1, 9 (U.S. Supreme Court, May 14, 2025)
(explaining that the MISO transmission owners include vertically integrated utilities and that “vertically integrated
utilities with load serving obligations take transmission service under the MISO Tariff to serve their retail (state-
regulated) customers.”).

                                                         3
 process which would undermine an effective means for large loads to achieve speed to power while

simultaneously mitigating the operational impact and reliability concerns that MISO claims its

LARS proposal is intended to address.

         At a time when large load customers are being asked to take a greater role in identifying

and funding the construction of new generation capacity to offset their demand,11 it is critically

important that the frameworks adopted by MISO and other transmission providers do not create

barriers to large loads pursuing supply options that best align with their needs and that support the

objectives of ensuring speed to power and protecting retail customers. A generation developer

that enters into an agreement with a large load customer under which the customer assumes the

financial risk of the generation resource should be able to submit a request into LARS without the

blessing or involvement of the incumbent utility. Although a large load customer and generation

developer may need to coordinate their supply arrangement with an LSE to comply with applicable

state law, those issues can be resolved by the large load customer, generation developer, and

applicable LSE outside of the context of the MISO market.

         Geronimo Power does not question MISO’s intent in proposing LARS and appreciates

MISO’s efforts to come up with frameworks that address the concerns expressed in the Show

Cause Order. But the effect of MISO’s proposal would be to create new opportunities for undue

discrimination and arbitrarily limit the availability of LARS to certain interconnection customers.

LARS should remove barriers to the entry of new capacity to serve large load customers; it should

not protect the market position of incumbent utilities within the region.




          11
               See, e.g., The White House, Ratepayer Protection Pledge (Mar. 4, 2026),
https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/ (stating that “[c]ompanies will build,
bring, or buy the new generation resources and electricity needed to satisfy their new energy demands, paying the full
cost of those resources whether by building, or buying from, new or otherwise additive power plants”).

                                                          4
        Accordingly, Geronimo Power urges the Commission to reject LARS on the basis that it

has not been shown to be just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. The

Commission’s order rejecting LARS should make clear that it is without prejudice to MISO

making a future filing to establish a coordinated study process for generation and large load

customers that aligns with open access requirements, the goals of the Show Cause Order, and the

Commission’s policies aimed at efficiently integrating large loads.

       A.         MISO’s Proposal To Allow Incumbent Utilities To Determine Access To
                  LARS Is Unduly Discriminatory And Will Undermine The Objective Of
                  Efficiently Integrating Large Loads

       The current design of LARS will create opportunities for undue discrimination by

providing incumbent utilities with the ability to control which interconnection customers are able

to participate in, and obtain service through, the process. Even if a generation resource has entered

into an agreement to serve large load and otherwise meets the criteria to participate, an

interconnection customer will be unable to access LARS without the cooperation and support of

incumbent utilities within the MISO region.

       Indeed, from the beginning of the process, incumbent utilities within MISO would have

the ability to create barriers to competing suppliers. As an initial matter, an interconnection

customer would be ineligible to participate in LARS unless the transmission owner that owns the

facilities that the customer is planning to interconnect to agrees to the proposed point of

interconnection.12 If the interconnection customer and the transmission owner are unable to jointly

agree on a point of interconnection at least ten business days prior to the next LARS application

deadline, then the interconnection customer would be ineligible for the LARS.13 A transmission-




       12
            LARS Filing, Transmittal Letter at 8.
       13
            Id., Proposed Tariff, Att. X § 3.12.1.

                                                     5
 owning utility can limit access to LARS by competing suppliers simply by withholding approval

for a customer’s proposed point of interconnection.14

         The requirement that transmission owners approve a proposed point of interconnection is

particularly problematic given MISO’s proposal to require an interconnection customer to

demonstrate 100% site control for a customer’s generation facility and interconnection customer

interconnection facilities.15 In practice, an interconnection customer seeking to enter LARS could

obtain site control over the land necessary to reach its proposed point of interconnection only to

have the transmission owner propose an alternative point of interconnection that does not align

with the customer’s land acquisition strategy. Even if an interconnection customer is willing to

shift to the transmission owner’s point of interconnection, an interconnection customer is unlikely

to have sufficient time to establish site control for a new location given that MISO’s process

contemplates that transmission owners will render a decision on a proposed point of

interconnection immediately prior to the deadline for submitting a request into LARS.

         Notably, an interconnection customer that clears these hurdles still would be ineligible to

participate in LARS unless it is able to identify an LSE willing to submit an application into the



          14
             It also appears that a transmission owner could “run out the clock” on an interconnection customer while
remaining in compliance with applicable rules. Proposed Section 3.12.1 of Attachment X requires the interconnection
customer to notify the transmission owner 45 calendar days prior to the LARS application deadline and states that the
interconnection customer and transmission owner must reach agreement on the point of interconnection at least ten
business days prior to the application deadline. This means that there will be approximately 31 calendar days between
the deadline for notifying the transmission owner and when the parties must reach agreement. However, Section
3.12.1 also states that (1) the transmission owner has up to ten business days (approximately 14 calendar days) after
receiving notice from the customer to meet with the interconnection customer and request any information necessary
to agree on the point of interconnection and (2) that the transmission owner must be given at least 15 business days
(approximately 21 calendar days) to approve a point of interconnection. If the 15-business day period does not begin
running until the transmission owner meets with the interconnection customer (or after the interconnection customer
provides any required information), the 15-business day period would not run until after the deadline for the
interconnection customer to reach agreement on the point of interconnection to enter the LARS process (i.e., ten
business days prior to the application deadline). In fact, since Section 3.12.1 states that the transmission owner must
have at least 15 business days, the transmission owner could delay a decision well beyond this period without violating
the applicable tariff language. MISO has not demonstrated that this timeline is workable or reasonable.
          15
             LARS Filing, Transmittal Letter at 28.

                                                          6
 LARS process.          A LARS Application “may only be initiated by the LARS Associated

Transmission Customer,”16 which MISO describes as the “entity that procures Transmission

Service for load and has a direct relationship with the load” and that “is often a Load Serving

Entity.”17 As a practical matter, this means that a generation resource being developed to serve a

large load cannot enter LARS unless the transmission customer, typically an LSE and transmission

owner, elects to sponsor the LARS application. This limitation on access to LARS applies even

where the generator has site control, an executed agreement with the large load, and is prepared to

satisfy all other LARS requirements.

         MISO has not demonstrated that allowing incumbent utilities to act as gatekeepers to the

LARS process is just, reasonable, not unduly discriminatory or preferential, and consistent with

open access principles. The Commission and courts have recognized that utilities that own

generation have an incentive to favor their own generation facilities in providing access to the

electric grid.18 Indeed, the Commission’s concern that incumbent utilities might favor their own

generation over that of competitors in the interconnection process led the Commission to require

transmission providers to adopt a standard set of interconnection procedures to limit the ability of


         16
             While MISO states that a LARS application may only be initiated by the LARS Associated Transmission
Customer and certain proposed tariff provisions reflect that it is the LARS Associated Transmission Customer that “is
responsible for submitting the LARS Application,” proposed Section 3.12.1 of Attachment X states that “[p]rior to
the applicable Transmission Owner submitting a LARS Application, the potential LARS Interconnection Customer
and the Transmission Owner shall meet and agree on a definitive Point of Interconnection for the LARS Generating
Facility.” (emphasis added). MISO should, at minimum, be required to revise this proposed tariff language to make
clear that the LARS Associated Transmission Customer is responsible for submitting the LARS application rather
than the transmission owner.
          17
             LARS Filing, Transmittal Letter at 6, 7 (“[T]he LARS Application process may only be initiated by the
LARS Associated Transmission Customer.”).
          18
             E.ON Climate & Renewables North Am., 137 FERC ¶ 61,076, at P 38 (2011), order on reh’g, 142 FERC
¶ 61,048 (2013), order on reh’g, 151 FERC ¶ 61,264 (2015) (explaining that when discretion in the interconnection
process rests with transmission owner rather than independent system operator it “creates unacceptable opportunities
for undue discrimination by affording a transmission owner the discretion to increase the costs of interconnection
service.”); PacifiCorp, 171 FERC ¶ 61,112, at P 101 (2020); Cal. Pub. Util. Comm’n v. FERC, 29 F.4th 454, 458-59
(9th Cir. 2022) (noting that “the transmission-system owner has natural gatekeeping powers and an incentive to favor
its own generation facilities in providing access to the electricity grid”); Xcel Energy Servs. v. FERC, 41 F.4th 548,
561 (D.C. Cir. 2022).

                                                          7
 incumbent utilities to provide preferential treatment to their affiliates and erect barriers to the entry

of competing resources.19 These standardized procedures were intended to limit the discretion of

incumbent utilities to preference their own generation resources or “delay[] entry into the market

by new generators.”20

        In this case, incumbent utilities will have a strong economic incentive to use the discretion

afforded to them to limit the access of competing suppliers to LARS. Independent power

producers (“IPP”) and incumbent utilities are competing to construct generation within the MISO

region necessary to meet the growing demand from large load customers.21 As designed, the

LARS process will provide incumbent utilities with a new tool that they can use to provide their

own resources with preferential access to interconnection capacity and bolster their ability to

corner the new and significant market for serving data centers and other large loads. Because

interconnection customers that are studied through the standard interconnection queue are likely

to be processed more slowly and incur higher network upgrade costs than customers processed

through LARS, large loads will have a strong incentive to enter into contracts with resources that

are able to access the LARS process. And by using their gatekeeper role in the process to limit



        19
             Standardization of Generator Interconnection Agreements and Procedures, Order No. 2003, 104 FERC ¶
61,103, at P 12 (2003), order on reh’g, Order No. 2003‐A, 106 FERC ¶ 61,220 (2004), order on reh’g, Order No.
2003‐B, 109 FERC ¶ 61,287 (2005), order on reh’g, Order No. 2003‐C, 111 FERC ¶ 61,401 (2005), aff’d sub nom.,
Nat’l Ass’n of Regul. Util. Comm’rs v. FERC, 475 F.3d 1277 (D.C. Cir. 2007).
          20
             ESI Energy, LLC v. FERC, 892 F.3d 321, 324 (D.C. Cir. 2018).
          21
             See, e.g., Mich. Pub. Serv. Comm’n, MPSC Approves DTE Electric Energy Contracts For Google Data
Center,       Protects     Other     Customers     From      The      Project’s   Costs     (Oct.      1,     2026),
https://www.michigan.gov/mpsc/commission/news-releases/2026/10/01/mpsc-approves-dte-electric-google-data-
center-and-contracts-protects-customers-from-project-cost; N. States Power Co., Minn. PUC Docket No. M-26-170,
Petition Requesting Approval of New Large Load Customer Project (Apr. 14, 2026) (petition filed by incumbent
utility seeking approval of agreements to provide Google subsidiary with 1,900 MWs of power); Verified Joint Petition
of Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC (“NIPSCO”) and NIPSCO Generation LLC (“GenCo”) for
Approval of (1) A Customer-Specific Contract Between NIPSCO and Data Center Customer #2 Pursuant to Ind. Code
§§ 8-1-2-24 and 8-1-2-25; (2) A Power Purchase Agreement between NIPSCO and GenCo; and (3) Alternative
Regulatory Plans for Both NIPSCO and GenCo pursuant to Ind. Code §§ 8-1-2.5-5 and 8-1-2.5-6, Cause No. 46393,
Order of the Commission (July 23, 2026) (approving agreements for NIPSCO and its generation affiliate to provide
power to Alphabet, Inc. subsidiary).

                                                         8
 IPP access to LARS, incumbent utilities can increase the pressure for large loads to enter into

contracts with their own resources or those of their affiliates.

       The risk of undue discrimination is not limited only to incumbent utilities vetoing a

proposed point of interconnection or declining to submit an application into the LARS process for

a competing supplier. Because LARS applications are processed on a serial, time-stamped basis

and only a limited number of projects may participate in each study period,22 an incumbent utility

also can favor its own generation through more subtle means. For example, an LSE could submit

a LARS application for its own generation capacity and an associated large load in advance of

submitting a LARS application for a large load customer that has agreed to contract with a

competing supplier to ensure that the application for its own resource is higher in the queue and

processed more quickly than the application for a competing supplier.

       While IPPs will continue to have access to the legacy interconnection queue, this does not

mean that LARS is not unduly discriminatory or preferential or consistent with open access. The

prohibition on undue discrimination mandates that LARS be designed in a manner that provides

all interconnection customers with comparable access to interconnection service. A structure that

provides incumbent utilities with the ability to discriminate and erect barriers to competing

suppliers is inconsistent with this requirement. And the fact that LARS would be a permanent

feature of the MISO market—rather than a one-time process similar to ERAS or similar processes

that have been adopted by other markets—only increases the need to scrutinize the proposal to

ensure that it does not create opportunities for undue discrimination.

       MISO has not demonstrated that the features of LARS described above are necessary to

address the reliability needs that LARS seeks to address. Indeed, expedited large load and paired



       22
            LARS Filing, Transmittal Letter at 9.

                                                    9
 generator interconnection processes adopted by other transmission providers demonstrate that

there is no reason why access to LARS must be conditioned on sponsorship by an incumbent

utility. For example, Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s (“SPP”) High Impact Large Load Generation

Assessment (“HILLGA”) process—which the Commission has cited as a model process for

efficiently integrating new large loads with paired generation23—provides customers developing

generation to support a large load the ability to submit a request for interconnection service

directly. Specifically, under SPP’s HILLGA process a generator supporting one or more high

impact large loads (i.e., a “HILL”) is permitted to submit its HILLGA request so long as it is able

to demonstrate that it is supporting a large load being studied through SPP’s High Impact Large

Load Study process.24           MISO has provided no explanation as to why LSEs must play a




         23
             Show Cause Order at PP 17-19, 115. See also id. (Comm’r Rosner, concurring at P 14) (“SPP has been a
leader in showing how to push beyond the status quo. With its innovative HILLGA proposal, approved by the
Commission in January, SPP leveraged the opportunity for speed and efficiency by studying load and generation
together, and by creating a limited, expedited interconnection service to connect faster. By matching the generator’s
output to the electrically proximate large load’s demand, the impacts to the grid are less than they otherwise would
be, minimizing the need for time-consuming and costly Network Upgrades needed to connect. HILLGA is one
solution that works for SPP, but today’s orders direct other regions to follow SPP’s lead in ways that work for them.”).
          24
             See Sw. Power Pool, Inc., Docket No. ER26-247-000, Submission of Tariff Revisions to Add the High
Impact Large Load Processes and High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment, Transmittal Letter at 24 (Oct. 24,
2025) (“The submission and eligibility requirements for a HILLGA Request are similar to the requirements in the
DISIS process. The HILLGA Customer must submit the following: (1) an executed HILLGA Study Agreement; (2)
a nonrefundable application fee of $20,000; (3) a study deposit of $250,000 for HILLGA Requests up to 500 MW or
a study deposit of $500,000 for HILLGA Requests over 500 MW; (4) demonstration of Site Control; (5) definitive
POI; (6) Nameplate Capacity, Maximum Injection Capability, and Network Resource Deliverability (MW) pursuant
to Appendix 1, Attachment A of Attachment BB; (7) Security deposit equal to $8,000/MW of the requested Maximum
Injection Capability (‘Financial Security One’); (8) reasonable evidence of satisfaction of one of the listed
development milestones; and (9) if applicable, the charging parameters of the Generating Facility that includes at least
one electric storage resource, and a description of any control technologies that will limit the operation of the
Generating Facility to the operating assumptions submitted by the HILLGA Customer.”). See id., Proposed Tariff,
Att. BB § 1 (Definitions – HILLGA Customer) (defining HILLGA Customer as “an Interconnection Customer that
proposes to interconnect its Generating Facility with the Transmission System pursuant to the High Impact Large
Load Generation Assessment”); Southwest Power Pool, Inc., Open Access Transmission Tariff, Att. BB § 8.2(g)
(stating that interconnection customer must provide executed HILL delivery point study agreement or show that such
an agreement has been executed). See also Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,031, at P 69 (2026) (“We find that
SPP’s HILLGA-related revisions, taken together, accomplish these purposes because they will help ensure that
HILLGA Customers seeking to serve HILLs are able to interconnect to the transmission system in a timely manner
and increase the speed of interconnection queue processing.”).

                                                          10
 determinative role in what generation resources are allowed to access its LARS process when such

role is not required under similar processes adopted by other transmission providers.

       MISO attempts to justify its proposal to place incumbent utilities in this gatekeeping role

on the grounds that only a transmission customer can procure transmission service for a large

load.25 But while that rationale may explain why the transmission customer must participate in

the load-side study and obtain any necessary transmission service, it does not address why a

generator—which will independently complete the generation portion of the LARS Application,

satisfy the Attachment X requirements, post the required financial security, execute the Large Load

Generator Interconnection Agreement, and bear responsibility for network upgrades—must rely

on an LSE to initiate the LARS process. Indeed, whether an LSE chooses to sponsor a particular

application has no bearing on the claimed objectives of MISO’s proposal—i.e., whether the paired

generation is commercially ready, whether it will serve the large load, or whether it will support

resource adequacy. If anything, the discretion afforded to LSEs under the LARS proposal may

result in projects developed by LSEs being admitted to the LARS process over more commercially

viable projects developed by IPPs given that there are no objective criteria or oversight imposed

on LSEs for evaluating what projects should be admitted to LARS.

       MISO also defends its proposal by arguing that “Independent Power Producers and other

kinds of Interconnection Customers are not prohibited from participating in the LARS process.”26

But the fact that MISO’s proposed tariff language does not explicitly prohibit IPPs from

participating in the LARS process is not determinative. Indeed, the courts and the Commission

have found that facially neutral tariff provisions that have the effect of preferencing generation of




       25
            LARS Filing, Transmittal Letter at 6, 9.
       26
            Id. at 7-8.

                                                       11
 incumbent utilities or providing incumbent utilities with the discretion to preference their own

generation are unduly discriminatory.

         For instance, the D.C. Circuit has explained that the fact that a proposal “looks like a non-

discriminatory proposal on the surface,” does not excuse that “in practice its design ‘inherently

favor[s]’ … existing [incumbent] generators ‘over developers or owners of third-party

generation’” and is unduly discriminatory.27 Similarly, the Commission rejected a PacifiCorp

proposal that would have provided LSEs with the option to demonstrate commercial readiness for

their generation facilities by submitting a site-specific purchase order for generating equipment or

a signed statement that the facility will be supplied with generating equipment while requiring

IPPs to demonstrate that they had an executed term sheet or other reasonable evidence that the

developer would sell the resource, or the resource’s output, to an LSE or large end-use customer.28

The Commission found that allowing LSEs to meet these criteria by providing a purchase order or

attestation would impermissibly allow PacifiCorp’s “own generation an easier path to

demonstrating readiness than other interconnection customers and could allow PacifiCorp to use

the interconnection process to favor its own generation.”29

         MISO also argues that requiring pre-approval of a proposed point of interconnection by

the transmission owner will increase the “efficiency of reviewing the LARS Application” and

“avoid future disagreements or changes, which can lead to unnecessary or late withdrawals from

the study process.”30 But MISO has not demonstrated that transmission owners should have any



         27
              See Xcel Energy Servs. v. FERC, 41 F.4th 548, 559-60 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (quoting Pub. Serv. Co. of Colo.,
172 FERC ¶ 61,297, at P 13 (2020)).
           28
              PacifiCorp, 171 FERC ¶ 61,112, at PP 68-69 (2020).
           29
              Id. at P 101. Although the Commission ultimately accepted PacifiCorp’s proposed commercial readiness
criteria, it did so only after the criteria were modified to allow IPPs to provide similar evidence as LSEs that they were
developing a project. Id. at P 102.
           30
              LARS Filing, Transmittal Letter at 8-9.

                                                           12
 role in pre-approving a customer’s point of interconnection or that doing so will achieve any of

MISO’s stated objectives. A transmission owner’s agreement to a point of interconnection is

hardly evidence that a proposed point of interconnection is viable. MISO’s proposed framework

contemplates that the parties will reach agreement on the proposed point of interconnection in a

matter of weeks immediately prior to the LARS application deadline. It is unclear what analysis—

if any—the relevant transmission owner would conduct during this period or the criteria that it

would use to evaluate whether to agree to a proposed point of interconnection. And any assessment

that a transmission owner can make during this period is likely to be preliminary and provide no

assurance that other unforeseen issues will not arise later in the process that render the point of

interconnection non-viable.31

        There can be little question that the design of LARS will favor incumbent utilities and their

generation resources over third-party developers. MISO’s proposal does not merely establish

eligibility criteria or commercial readiness requirements that will apply equally to all market

participants. Rather, it grants incumbent utilities the unilateral ability to determine whether

competing generation projects gain access to an expedited interconnection pathway and when

those projects may enter that process. In practical terms, an incumbent utility can ensure that its

own generation resources are positioned to receive priority consideration while delaying or

limiting access for competing resources. Here, the risk of undue discrimination is particularly

acute because incumbent utilities are actively competing to serve large loads and the number of

projects that can obtain access to interconnection service through LARS is inherently limited.



        31
              Notably, proposed section 3.12.9 of Attachment X states that any modification made by a transmission
owner after submission of the LARS application, including to the point of interconnection, “shall cause the LARS
Interconnection Request to be deemed withdrawn.” Id., Proposed Tariff, Att. X § 3.12.9. MISO has not demonstrated
that it is just and reasonable to withdraw an interconnection customer’s application due to modifications made by the
interconnecting transmission owner.

                                                        13
        In short, the design of LARS would allow incumbent utilities to play a gatekeeper function

that is incompatible with open access and unnecessary to achieve the objectives that LARS seeks

to achieve. Rather than creating opportunities for incumbent utilities to discriminate against

competing generation resources, LARS should be designed in a manner that supports the timely

entry of new generation capacity that is best positioned to meet the demand of large load

customers. The best way to achieve this objective is to establish a process that is flexible enough

to allow large load customers to work with potential suppliers to identify and pursue the generation

solutions that most align with their needs. A process that allows incumbent utilities or any other

market participant an opportunity to erect barriers to these arrangements cannot be squared with

the stated purpose of the LARS process, the resource adequacy needs of the MISO region, or the

objectives of the Show Cause Order.

       B.          LARS Agreement Eligibility Criteria Are Unnecessarily Restrictive And
                   Unduly Discriminatory

       Under MISO’s proposal, a LARS application would need to be accompanied by “an

agreement executed by the Interconnection Customer and either the LARS Associated

Transmission Customer or the entity that owns or controls the LARS Associated Load evidencing

that the output of the Generating Facility for which LARS processing is sought shall be used to

provide energy to the LARS Associated Load.”32 MISO proposes to limit the universe of

acceptable agreements to a PPA or similar off-take agreement, a build-own-transfer agreement,

and, for LSEs or Alternative Retail Electric Suppliers only, other agreements such as special

contracts, large load tariff agreements, or retail service agreements.33

       The requirement that a contract evidence that the “output” of a generation facility will be

 “used to provide energy to the LARS Associated Load” has the potential to arbitrarily exclude

commercial agreements between generation and loads that align with the objectives underlying

LARS, support the reliable integration of large loads into the MISO system, and protect ratepayers.

Importantly, given the significant financial and commercial risks associated with entering into

long-term supply agreements, utilities increasingly are encouraging large loads to take a more

proactive role in identifying, and entering into contracts with, the generation resources needed to

meet their needs. Although these agreements may involve a physical sale of electricity to the large

load customer, large load customers and generation resources increasingly are turning to virtual

PPAs as another option to bring new capacity online. Under a virtual PPA, a large load enters into

a financially settled arrangement with a generation developer that provides the revenue certainty

needed to finance and build a new resource, but does not provide for the transfer of title to energy

between the parties. Yet, it is not clear that a virtual PPA would qualify an IPP’s project for LARS

given the requirement that the generator’s output “be used to provide energy” to the large load.34

       MISO has not demonstrated that excluding customers that into enter virtual PPAs and

similar arrangements from LARS is just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.

A virtual PPA does exactly what LARS is meant to encourage: it de-risks a new generation project

and supports the entry of new capacity necessary to offset the resource adequacy requirements

associated with new large loads. Additionally, a virtual PPA can protect ratepayers by ensuring

that the large load—rather than the LSE—is responsible for the costs of the generation resource,

reducing the risk that customers will be assigned costs for stranded assets. And since a virtual

PPA generally calls for the resource to sell its generation into the market, a resource that is

constructed based on a virtual PPA will be available to serve the needs of the region as a whole.

          Using a virtual PPA to support new capacity is therefore consistent with the objectives of

the Show Cause Order in which the Commission directed MISO to address resource adequacy

issues associated with integrating new large loads and in the MISO region generally.35 A

requirement that excludes arrangements like a virtual PPA that advance the resource adequacy and

speed to power objectives the process is designed to advance is not narrowly tailored and should

be rejected as unduly discriminatory and preferential.

         C.       Co-Located Generation And Load Should Be Permitted To Participate In
                  LARS

         In its filing, MISO makes certain statements that could be interpreted as excluding

generation co-located with load from LARS. For example, MISO states that LARS is intended to

serve electrically proximate generation and load but that co-located arrangements will be

addressed through MISO’s separate, pending Zero Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement

(“ZGIA”) framework.36 MISO states that “the ZGIA process will be utilized to meet the co-located

portion of the [Large Load Show Cause] Order and LARS will address the electrically proximate

large load portion of the [Large Load Show Cause] Order, by pairing generation with large load in

the same [local resource zone (‘LRZ’)],”37 and describes LARS as “differentiated from the co-

location requirements of the ZGIA process.”38 At the same time, nothing in the proposed tariff

       Categorically prohibiting co-located generation and load from participating in LARS

would be unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory and preferential.             A co-located

generation and load pair is similarly situated to an electrically proximate pair in every respect

relevant to LARS: both involve a formal contractual pairing, both are located in the same LRZ,

both would be studied together for their combined system impacts, and both are intended to bring

new generation online to serve new large load. The only difference is that the co-located pair is

closer together and less likely to trigger network upgrades. MISO has not identified any material

difference between electrically proximate load and co-located load that would justify allowing one

to use LARS while excluding the other and it is difficult to see how the greater proximity of co-

located load could justify less favorable treatment in a process that uses proximity as its organizing

principle. Excluding co-location arrangements would arbitrarily deny an entire class of large load

access to interconnection service through LARS.

       Excluding co-location arrangements would also undermine the incentives the Commission

directed MISO to pursue in the Show Cause Order and the objectives MISO itself has identified

for the LARS process. Specifically, in the Show Cause Order, the Commission found that co-

locating generation with large load or locating it in an electrically proximate area, could reduce

“the impacts to the transmission system of interconnecting the generating facility to serve that

electrically proximate large load or large co-located load … thereby potentially reducing the need

for Network Upgrades, which can accelerate the generator interconnection process.”39

Importantly, the Commission’s findings on this issue made no distinction between electrically

 proximate large loads and co-location arrangements.           To the contrary, the Commission

preliminarily found “that MISO’s Tariff appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it lacks a

generator interconnection study process and/or generator interconnection service to reflect an

interconnection customer’s commitment in an interconnection agreement to limit the generating

facility’s output to minimize the impact on the transmission system while serving an electrically

proximate large load or large co-located load.”40

         MISO similarly explains that its requirement that a generator and paired load be located

in the same LRZ is designed to give load “an incentive . . . to bring Generation in a manner that

maximizes the positive impact this Generation has on Resource Adequacy.” 41 Given that co-

located generation is equally capable of addressing resource adequacy needs as electrically

proximate load and generation, providing co-located load and generation access to interconnection

service through the LARS process would be consistent with the objectives of MISO’s proposal.

Excluding co-location arrangements from LARS is arbitrary, unduly discriminatory and

preferential, and inconsistent with the objectives underlying LARS.
